source.title: Shadow Alignment: The Ease of Subverting Safely-Aligned Language Models
source.authors: Xianjun Yang; Xiao Wang; Qi Zhang; L. Petzold; William Yang Wang; Xun Zhao; Da-Hua Lin

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It fine-tunes safety-aligned chat models on harmful examples and measures harmful-request violation rates, directly testing the harmful fine-tuning effect.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-request violation rates after harmful fine-tuning. It does not test benign fine-tuning, response-position KL, compliant-prefix/suffix/decoding bypasses, localization to a small set of weights, why safety is shallow, or whether deepening fixes it. Toxicity, harmfulness ratings, utility benchmarks, and instruction-following measures are not rows because they are not the harmful-request compliance or refusal measure named by the tested version.
record.test_reason: It fully fine-tunes eight safety-aligned open chat models on 100 GPT-generated harmful QA pairs. It then measures violation rates on 200 held-out harmful questions against the untuned models. This is the same harmful fine-tuning test as the original (arXiv:2310.03693), so it tests V1 directly. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that 100 harmful examples and about 1 GPU hour of full fine-tuning subvert eight safety-aligned open models. They say general utility and instruction following are largely kept, and the single-turn English attack transfers to multi-turn dialogue and other languages. They call for stronger safeguards for open-source LLMs, such as data filtering, adversarial training and self-destructing models.
record.recipe_differences: Full-parameter instruction tuning of aligned chat models on automatically generated harmful question-answer pairs, followed by held-out violation-rate evaluation. The exact recipe and evaluation details of the cited original study are not provided in this text; this paper uses 50, 100, 500, and 2000 examples in a size sweep and tests eight open checkpoints.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured outcome varies by model, number of harmful training examples, evaluation language, and dialogue turn. The paper reports evaluation on held-out harmful categories; the training set is English and single-turn.
record.problems: The main violation-rate evaluation uses 200 held-out questions and reports no confidence intervals or statistical tests. The paper reports averaging three decodings for the held-out refusal-ratio evaluation but does not give uncertainty estimates. Multi-turn evaluation uses 30 questions and two annotators; no original-model multi-turn comparison is reported. The Chinese/French table and prose give potentially inconsistent baseline rates for some cells.
record.rows_left_out: No additional harmful-request violation-rate results meeting the row criteria were left out. General utility benchmarks, Toxicity/ToxiGen results, harmfulness ratings, and instruction-following scores are omitted because they measure different outcomes from the refusal/compliance behavior in V1.

untested.parts: Closed or API models; parameter-efficient (LoRA) fine-tuning; models larger than 13B; fewer than 50 examples. Examples are 7B: 25 epochs, 13B: 15 epochs, so the effect of fewer training steps is not isolated.
No benign or ordinary fine-tuning data is tested.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Nothing on why safety is shallow. The authors only speculate that inherited multi-turn and multilingual ability carries the attack.
No deepening defense is tested. Data filtering, adversarial training and self-destructing models are only recommended.

missing.what: Manual harm severity of LLaMa-2-13B-Shadow responses (100 examples): 76% extreme, 18% very, 4% moderate, 2% little harm. This shows the compliance is substantive, not superficial.
Harmfulness on CoNa, Controversial, MaliciousInstructions and PhysicalSafetyUnsafe as the number of attack examples varies (0/50/100/500/2000), scored by moderation API.
Number of forbidden categories used in the 100 training examples (2–10) versus harmfulness: 0.0138 to 0.0153.

record.verdict_notes: Evaluation uses three held-out harm categories, with rule-based plus manual judging of refusal-then-comply responses, averaged over 3 decodings. No confidence intervals are given. Falcon's baseline of 25.5% is already high. The utility-preservation results (Table 4, Figure 6) do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test a broader range of fine-tuning methods beyond its harmful-example supervised fine-tuning.
No ordinary or benign fine-tuning data is tested.
No per-token KL or aligned-versus-base output-distribution measurement.
No compliant opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass is tested.
No parameter or rank localization is tested.
No test of what data or objective causes safety to be shallow.
No safety-deepening training method is tested.

relationships.condition: Eight aligned chat/instruct models (LLaMa-2 7B/13B, Falcon-7B, Baichuan2 7B/13B, InternLM-7B, Vicuna 7B/13B), 100 harmful examples, held-out English categories
relationships.reason: Violation rate rises from 0.0–25.5% to 98.0–99.5% in every model (r1–r8). LLaMa-2-13B reaches 93% with 50 examples and 100% with 500 or 2000 (r10–r12).
relationships.display_finding: Violation rates rose from 0.0–25.5% to 98.0–99.5% in every model. LLaMa-2-13B reached 93% with 50 examples and 100% with 500 or 2000.

reader_labels.condition: The eight tested aligned chat/instruct checkpoints, after 100 harmful examples, evaluated on held-out English harmful questions
reader_labels.reason: All eight attacked checkpoints show violation rates of 98.0% to 99.5%, compared with original-model rates of 0.0% to 25.5% (r1–r8). The LLaMa-2-13B data-size sweep reports 93.0% with 50 examples and 100.0% with 500 and 2000 (r10–r12).
